OpenClaw Multi-Agent Sandbox: Isolate Agents on One VPS

Build and test an OpenClaw multi-agent sandbox with separate credentials, Docker boundaries, Tailscale, socat, Discord, and escape checks.

March 7, 2026
·
Erwan Lee PesleFounder, Casys AI
·
Updated on 8/1/2026
Tagged — click to explore
#openclaw#agent-sandbox#multi-agent-sandbox#security#docker#tailscale#discord

Stuck on something like this?

Bring the blocker. We frame the problem before talking tools.

calendar_monthBook 20 min with Erwan

Short answer: a useful OpenClaw multi-agent sandbox is not one switch. It is a chain of explicit boundaries: separate gateways, identities and credentials; constrained filesystem and process execution; a narrow network path; authorized messaging; and negative tests that prove forbidden paths fail.

Two agents need to work in the same Discord channel and on the same VPS. Agent A belongs to one operator; Agent B belongs to another. Each operator also has a private assistant with access to personal messages, calendars and client work. The collaboration agents need enough freedom to edit code and run tests, but no path back to those private assets.

That sounds like a container problem. It is actually a trust-boundary problem. Docker can constrain tool execution. Tailscale can provide authenticated network connectivity. socat can relay a TCP stream. Discord can route messages. None of them, alone or together, decides every authorization question.

This tutorial builds the boundaries in dependency order and ends with the evidence required to call the setup isolated.

What This OpenClaw Multi-Agent Sandbox Builds

The topology has four zones:

  1. Operator A keeps a private OpenClaw Gateway and a dedicated collaboration agent.
  2. Operator B does the same in a separate trust boundary.
  3. Both collaboration agents join one allowlisted Discord channel.
  4. Both reach one disposable VPS through a deliberately narrow SSH path.

OpenClaw’s security guidance assumes one trusted operator boundary per Gateway. It does not describe one shared Gateway as a hostile multi-tenant boundary. If the two owners do not fully trust each other, keep separate Gateways and preferably separate OS users or hosts. The shared VPS is the collaboration surface, not a container for both owners’ private credentials.

The definition of done is behavioral: each collaboration agent can reach its Discord channel and its own VPS account, while attempts to read a private workspace, invoke host execution, reuse the other agent’s credentials or reach an unapproved network destination fail.

Step 1: Map the Trust Boundaries

Write down the boundary before writing configuration:

ZoneSensitive assetsAllowed crossing
Private AMain-agent workspace, channel sessions, model and service credentialsMain A may delegate to local Collab A
Private BMain-agent workspace, channel sessions, model and service credentialsMain B may delegate to local Collab B
Shared DiscordCollaboration messages and attachmentsListed humans and the two bot identities, in one channel
Shared VPSDisposable repository, build output and test servicesSSH to one dedicated Unix account per agent

This map prevents a common category error: reachability is not permission. A packet reaching the VPS proves connectivity. The SSH account, filesystem ownership and application rules still decide what that connection may do.

Step 2: Separate Identities and Credentials

Use a distinct identity at every layer:

LayerAgent AAgent BNever share
OpenClawcollab-a agent and workspacecollab-b agent and workspaceAgent directory or private workspace
DiscordBot A tokenBot B tokenOne bot token between owners
TailscaleGateway A device identityGateway B device identityReusable enrollment credentials
VPSUnix user and SSH key for AUnix user and SSH key for Broot login or one private key

OpenClaw stores authentication by agent, but its documentation notes that a secondary agent without a local profile can read through to the default agent’s auth profiles. Do not treat a different agent ID as proof of credential separation. Populate only the credentials the collaboration agent needs; for stronger separation, run the owners’ Gateways under separate OS accounts or hosts.

Keep Discord tokens out of prompts, repositories and agent workspaces. OpenClaw supports environment-backed SecretRefs. Give each Gateway a different variable, such as DISCORD_COLLAB_A_TOKEN and DISCORD_COLLAB_B_TOKEN.

On the VPS, create non-root accounts such as collab_a and collab_b. Give each one its own SSH public key and working directory. If both agents need one repository, use an explicit Unix group or repository permissions. Do not solve collaboration by giving both keys unrestricted root access.

Step 3: Isolate Filesystem and Process Execution

Configure the collaboration agent explicitly. This example starts with no network so the filesystem and process boundary can be tested before connectivity is added:

The controls do different jobs:

  • mode: "all" routes that agent’s tool execution through the sandbox backend.
  • scope: "agent" gives the agent its own runtime. Use session if separate sessions must not share runtime state; never use shared for this boundary.
  • workspaceAccess: "rw" exposes one selected host workspace read-write. It does not expose other host directories.
  • readOnlyRoot, writable tmpfs paths and capDrop: ["ALL"] restrict the container runtime while preserving a place for temporary files.
  • the tool deny list removes control-plane and browser capabilities; disabling elevated execution closes the documented host-exec escape hatch.

This is risk reduction, not a mathematical guarantee. The Gateway and native plugins still run outside the Docker sandbox. A bind mount pierces the filesystem boundary for the exact host path it exposes, and a Docker socket mount effectively hands host control to the container. Review every mount and never mount /var/run/docker.sock into the agent sandbox.

If the agent needs ssh, bake openssh-client into a custom sandbox image. Avoid temporarily making the root filesystem writable and enabling broad network access just to install packages during a run.

Apply and inspect the effective policy:

sandbox explain is the truth surface: check the resolved mode, scope, workspace access, mounts, tool policy and elevated gates. A config file that looks correct is not enough if an older container is still running with stale settings.

Step 4: Add Only the Required Network Path

OpenClaw’s Docker sandbox defaults to network: "none". Keep that default until the no-network test passes. Then add one path from the sandbox to SSH on the shared VPS.

Create a Dedicated Docker Bridge

Create a user-defined bridge and set the sandbox network to its name:

Recreate the sandbox after the change. A user-defined bridge separates attached containers from unrelated Docker networks, but it does not automatically restrict Internet egress or authorize the VPS. Enforce the desired egress policy in the host firewall and test it from inside the sandbox.

Relay One Port with socat

If the host can reach the VPS through Tailscale but the sandbox should not join the tailnet, a host relay can expose only SSH to the Docker bridge:

Discover the bridge gateway and subnet with docker network inspect; do not assume 172.17.0.1. Bind the listener to that bridge address, not 0.0.0.0, restrict accepted source addresses, and add a host firewall rule for the same source and port.

socat is a bidirectional byte relay. It does not authenticate the agent, encrypt the SSH payload or decide which Unix account may log in. The localhost trap explains the namespace side of this bridge; the security boundary comes from the narrow listener, the host firewall, Tailscale policy and SSH authorization together.

Restrict the Tailscale Path

Tailscale creates authenticated, encrypted connectivity between nodes. It does not mean every node should reach every other node. In a new tailnet, the default policy can allow all devices to communicate until you replace it. Define a narrow grant, for example:

Grants and ACLs are additive: remove any broader rule that would still match these devices, because adding this narrow grant does not revoke an existing path. This grant authorizes a network connection to port 22. It does not replace the dedicated SSH users, keys, command restrictions or filesystem permissions on the VPS.

Step 5: Authorize Agent Communication

There are two different communication paths:

  • sessions_send is an OpenClaw session tool inside one Gateway. Cross-agent targeting is separately controlled by tools.agentToAgent, and session visibility is controlled by tools.sessions.visibility.
  • Discord is the cross-Gateway collaboration channel. Its bot identity, guild, channel, sender and mention policies determine which messages can trigger each collaboration agent.

Do not describe sessions_send as a protocol between independent OpenClaw installations. If the workflow needs durable cross-process orchestration instead of a shared chat channel, see ACPX multi-agent orchestration.

On each Gateway, configure its own bot token and route only the shared channel to the collaboration agent:

Use numeric Discord IDs so openclaw channels status --probe can audit permissions. allowBots: "mentions", sender allowlists and requireMention: true reduce accidental bot-to-bot triggering. They are not a proof that loops are impossible; keep OpenClaw’s loop protection enabled, cap work at the workflow layer and monitor logs.

Allowlists authorize who may trigger the agent. They do not make channel topics, messages or attachments trusted instructions.

Step 6: Run Escape Tests and Keep the Evidence

A sandbox is credible when both positive and negative tests pass. Run these after every policy, image, mount, network or routing change:

BoundaryTestPassing evidence
RoutingMessage from an unlisted user, then a listed user without a mentionNo agent run for either message; a listed, mentioned message creates exactly one run
Private filesAsk Collab A to read a canary outside its mounted workspacePath is absent or denied; sandbox explain and docker inspect show no private mount
Root filesystemTry to create a file under /usr/local/binWrite fails while writes inside the selected workspace succeed
Host controlTry elevated or Gateway executionTool policy rejects it; no host-side process appears
Docker controlTest for /var/run/docker.sock inside the sandboxSocket is absent
NetworkConnect to the relay, then to an unapproved host and portRelay succeeds; unapproved destination fails according to firewall and tailnet policy
VPS identityUse A’s credential for A’s account, then for B’s account and rootA succeeds only for its account; the other logins fail
RestartRecreate the sandbox and repeat the suiteResults stay identical with the new runtime

Useful operator evidence includes:

Store the effective config hash, command output, timestamp and expected result with the deployment record. A screenshot of one successful SSH session proves availability, not isolation.

What the Architecture Proves, and What It Does Not

ControlWhat it establishesWhat it does not establish
OpenClaw sandbox + DockerA constrained place for tool execution, files and processesA perfect security boundary or isolation of the host Gateway and native plugins
Tailscale grantWhich tagged sources may open a network connection to VPS port 22Permission to log in, become root or access an application
socat relayOne TCP path between two addressesAuthentication, encryption or command authorization
Discord policiesWhich identities and channel events may trigger the routed agentTrust in message content or a guarantee against every loop
VPS Unix accountsOS-level identity and filesystem/process permissionsSafe agent behavior or protection from an unpatched kernel/service

This separation is the central lesson: isolation limits where code runs, connectivity defines what can be reached, and authorization decides what an authenticated identity may do. Treating those as one feature produces attractive diagrams and weak systems.

Definition of Done

The OpenClaw multi-agent sandbox is ready only when:

  • each owner has a separate Gateway trust boundary;
  • collaboration agents have distinct workspaces, bot tokens and VPS accounts;
  • effective sandbox policy and mounts match the intended filesystem/process boundary;
  • elevated execution and Docker socket access are absent;
  • the only required network path is documented and tested;
  • Tailscale and host firewall policy restrict reachability, while SSH still authorizes the user;
  • Discord routing, sender allowlists and mention gating pass positive and negative tests;
  • all escape tests are rerun after recreation or restart;
  • operators retain the evidence instead of relying on configuration intent.

For the operational loop around these checks, read Loop engineering is a workflow.
